en: First Chapter:
Having bowed my head to Viṣṇu, the Lord and Sovereign of the three worlds, I shall here extract this Compendium of Royal Policy from the ocean of various treatises. (1)

O best of beings, that man who has studied according to the scriptures understands the renowned instruction on dharma, as well as what ought and ought not to be done, and what is auspicious and inauspicious. ||2||
Therefore, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, I shall fully explain that by the mere knowledge of which one attains omniscience. (3)
Even a wealthy man comes to ruin through instructing foolish disciples, supporting a wicked wife, and associating with those who are suffering. (4)
A wicked wife, a deceitful friend, a servant who speaks back, and living in a house with snakes—these are nothing but death for us; of this there is no doubt. (5)
One should save wealth for times of misfortune, and protect one's wife even at the cost of wealth;
however, one should always protect oneself, even at the cost of both wife and wealth. (6)
One should save wealth for times of misfortune; for what misfortunes do not befall even the prosperous?
Fortune may depart at any time, and even that which has been accumulated perishes.
In that country where there is no respect, no means of livelihood, no kinsmen, and no acquisition of knowledge, one should not make one's residence. (8)
A wealthy man, a learned brahmin, a king, a river, and fifthly a physician—if these five are not found in a place, one should not dwell there for even a single day. (9)
Where these five are not found—concern for worldly conduct, fear, shame, courtesy, and a disposition toward generosity—one should not establish a connection there. (10)
One should know servants by their dispatching of tasks, kinsmen by the arrival of misfortune, a friend in times of calamity, and a wife when wealth has been exhausted. (11)
He who stands by one when afflicted by illness, when calamity has arrived, during famine, in the peril of enemies, at the king’s gate, or in the cremation ground—he alone is a kinsman. (12)
He who abandons certainties and pursues uncertainties loses his certainties; for that which is uncertain is already lost. (13)
A wise man should marry a girl born of a noble family even if she is ill-favored;
however, there should be no marriage for one of low status with a girl of beautiful form and good character from a high-ranking family. 14.
One should never place trust in rivers, in those with weapons in hand, in those with claws, in those with horns, nor likewise in women or in royal families. (15)
Nectar should be taken even from poison, gold even from filth, supreme knowledge even from a low person, and a jewel of a woman even from a base family. (16)
The food of women is said to be twofold, their modesty fourfold, their recklessness sixfold, and their desire eightfold. (17)
The Second Chapter: Untruthfulness, rashness, deceit, folly, excessive greed, impurity, and mercilessness—these are the innate defects of women. (1)
Delicious food and the power to eat it, a beautiful woman and the power for sexual enjoyment, wealth and the power to give charity—these are not the fruits of meager austerity. (2)
He whose son is self-controlled, whose wife follows his will,
and who is content with his wealth— for him, heaven indeed exists even here on earth.
They are sons who are devoted to their father; he is a father who provides nourishment.
He is a friend in whom there is trust; she is a wife in whom there is peace.
One who destroys one's work behind one's back, yet speaks kindly to one's face.
One should avoid such a friend as one would a jar of poison with milk on its surface.
One should not trust a bad friend, nor should one trust even a good friend;
for at some time, a provoked friend may reveal all one's secrets. (6)
One should not reveal with speech a task conceived in the mind;
one should protect it secretly through counsel and then apply oneself to the task.
Folly is indeed miserable, and youth is indeed miserable;
but dwelling in another's house is even more miserable than misery itself. (8)
There is no ruby on every mountain, nor pearl in every elephant;
there are not saints everywhere, nor sandalwood in every forest. (9)
Sons should always be directed toward various virtues by the wise;
those who are knowledgeable in ethics and endowed with good character become honored by their lineage. (10)
A mother who is an enemy and a father who is a foe is he by whom a child has not been taught;
such a person does not shine in the midst of an assembly, just as a crane does not shine in the midst of swans.
From pampering arise many faults, while from striking arise many virtues;
therefore, one should strike both a son and a disciple, and not indulge them.
One should make each day fruitful through acts of giving, study, and ritual performance, whether by means of a verse, half a verse, or even a quarter-verse. 13.
Separation from a beloved, humiliation by one's own kin,
the remnants of battle, and service to a wicked king.
Poverty and an unfavorable assembly—these burn your body even without fire. (14)
Trees on the riverbank, women in the houses of others, and kings devoid of ministers—these undoubtedly perish quickly. (15)
The strength of Brahmins is knowledge, the strength of kings is their army, the strength of Vaiśyas is wealth, and the strength of Śūdras is service. (16)
O King, a courtesan abandons a man who is penniless, a subject abandons one who has been defeated, birds abandon a tree that is devoid of fruit, and a guest abandons a house after having eaten. 17.
Having received their sacrificial fee, the Brahmins abandon the patron;
likewise, having acquired knowledge, the disciples abandon the teacher, just as deer abandon the forest once they have reached it. 18.
A man who is of evil conduct, evil vision, and difficult to dwell with—a wicked person—quickly perishes if friendship is formed with him by men. (19)
Affection shines in a state of equality; service shines in a king;
trade shines in business dealings; and a divine woman shines in the home. (20)
The Third Chapter:
Whose fault is there in this world? By whom has one not been afflicted by disease?
Who has not encountered calamity? And whose happiness is constant? (1)
Conduct reveals one's family; speech reveals one's country; eagerness reveals one's affection; and the body reveals one's diet. (2)
One should unite a daughter with a noble family, a son with branches of learning, an enemy with calamity, and a friend with dharma. ||3||
Between a wicked person and a snake, a snake is better than a wicked person;
for a snake bites only at the proper time, but a wicked person strikes at every step. (4)
For this very purpose, kings gather together those of noble lineage;
they do not abandon the king in the beginning, the middle, or at the end.
It is said that at the time of universal dissolution, the oceans indeed break their bounds;
yet even in dissolution, the oceans do not seek to transgress them, nor do the virtuous.
A fool, however, must be avoided; he is a two-legged beast perceived before one's eyes, who pierces with the pain of his words like an invisible thorn. (7)
Those endowed with beauty and youth, born of noble lineage, do not shine if devoid of learning, like *kiṃśuka* flowers without fragrance. (8)
The voice is the beauty of cuckoos; a devoted wife is the beauty of women; learning is the beauty of the ugly; and forbearance is the beauty of the wicked. (9)
One should abandon an individual for the sake of a family; one should abandon a family for the sake of a village;
one should abandon a village for the sake of a country; and one should abandon the entire earth for the sake of the self. ||10||
In exertion there is no poverty; for one who recites prayers, there is no sin;
through silence, there is no quarrel; and for one who remains awake, there is no fear. 11.
Sītā was indeed captivated by excessive beauty, and Rāvaṇa by excessive pride;
for one is bound by excessive giving—indeed, one should avoid excess in all things. (12)
What is too heavy for the capable? What is distant for the industrious? What is a foreign land for those with true knowledge? Who is a stranger to those who speak kindly? (13)
Even by a single fragrant tree being burned,
that entire forest is perfumed, just as a whole family is tainted by a bad son.
Just as an entire forest is consumed by fire ignited from a single dry tree, so too is a whole family destroyed by a wicked son. 15.
By even a single good son, who is virtuous and endowed with learning, the entire family is gladdened, just as the night is by the moon. (16)
What is the use of many sons who cause grief and torment? Better is one son who supports the lineage, upon whom the family finds its rest. (17)
One should fondle [the son] for five years, and for ten years one should discipline him;
but when the sixteenth year has arrived, one should treat the son like a friend.
In times of calamity, during the reign of another king, in famine, in terrifying danger, or in the company of wicked people—he who flees survives. (19)
For that mortal in whom not even one among dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa is found, there is in birth after birth nothing but death. (20)
Where fools are not honored, where grain is well-stored, and where there is no quarrel between husband and wife—there Prosperity has come of her own accord. (21)
The Fourth Chapter:
Lifespan, action, wealth, knowledge, and even death—these five are indeed created for the embodied being while still dwelling in the womb. (1)
From the virtuous, even sons, friends, and kinsmen turn away;
yet those who go along with them share in that merit, for through their righteousness the family prospers.
Just as the fish, the tortoise, and the bird constantly protect their young through sight, thought, and touch, so too does association with the virtuous. ||3||
As long as this body remains healthy and death is still far off, one should perform what is beneficial for the self; for what will one do when the end of life has come?
Knowledge indeed possesses the qualities of the wish-fulfilling cow, for it yields fruit even out of season;
like a mother during travel, knowledge is remembered as hidden wealth. (5)
Even a single virtuous son is better than hundreds who lack virtue;
a single moon dispels the darkness, whereas thousands of stars cannot.
A fool, though born to live long, is better than one who dies at birth;
for the latter dies with little suffering, whereas the dull-witted man causes torment throughout his entire life.
Dwelling in a wretched village, serving those of low birth,
eating poor food, and having a wife with a wrathful face.
A foolish son and a widowed daughter—
these two burn the body even without fire.
What is the use of that cow which neither gives milk nor bears calves?
What is the purpose of a son who is born but neither learned nor devoted? (9)
For those scorched by the miseries of saṃsāra, there are three causes of rest:
offspring, a wife, and the right path for the virtuous.
Kings speak but once; the wise speak but once;
daughters are given away but once—these three things happen only once.
Austerity is for one alone; study is for two; singing is for three;
traveling is for four; a field is for five; and battle is for many. (12)
She is a wife who is pure and skillful; she is a wife who is devoted to her husband;
she is a wife who is dear to her husband; she is a wife who speaks the truth. (13)
The house of one without a son is empty; the quarters are empty for one without kinsmen;
the heart of a fool is empty; but poverty is the emptiness of all things. (14)
Scripture is poison without practice; food is poison when undigested;
social gathering is poison for the poor; and a young woman is poison for the old. (15)
One should abandon dharma devoid of compassion; one should abandon a teacher devoid of knowledge;
one should abandon a wife whose face is set in anger; and one should abandon kinsmen who are devoid of affection. 16.
Travel is the aging of men; for horses, aging is being tethered;
for women, aging is celibacy; and for garments, aging is exposure to the sun. 17.
"What is the time? Who are my friends? What is the place? What are my expenditures and income? To whom do I belong? And what is my capacity?"—thus one should reflect again and again. (18)
Fire is the deity of the twice-born; for sages, the deity resides in the heart;
for those of small intellect, there is an image; but for those who see with equanimity everywhere, [the deity is omnipresent]. 19.
The Fifth Chapter:
Fire is the preceptor of the twice-born; the Brāhmaṇa is the preceptor of the social orders (varṇas);
the husband alone is the preceptor of women; and the guest is the preceptor of everyone. (1)
Just as gold is tested by four means— rubbing, cutting, heating, and striking—
so too is a person tested by four means.
By renunciation, by conduct, by virtue, and by action. ||2||
One should fear as long as danger has not yet arrived;
but having perceived that danger has arrived, one should strike back without hesitation.
Born from the same womb and born under the same constellation,
they do not possess equal characters, just like the thorns of the jujube tree.
One who is free from desire shall not be an official; one who lacks longing shall not be fond of ornaments;
one who is unrefined shall not speak kindly; and one who speaks clearly shall not be a deceiver.
The learned are hated by the foolish; the very wealthy are hated by the poor;
a beautiful woman is hated by women of noble family; and an auspicious wife is hated by those who are unfortunate.
Knowledge that has fallen into indolence, wealth that has passed into the hands of others, a field sown with few seeds, and an army without a leader—all these are lost. (7)
Knowledge is sustained by practice; family is sustained by character;
a noble person is known by their virtues; and anger is perceived by the eyes.
Dharma is protected by wealth; knowledge is protected by practice;
a king is protected by mildness; and a household is protected by a virtuous wife. (9)
Otherwise, his Vedic scholarship is one thing, his scriptural knowledge another, and his conduct yet another;
speaking in one way, the world suffers while he acts in quite another.
Generosity destroys poverty; ethical discipline destroys rebirth in miserable states;
wisdom destroys ignorance; and meditative cultivation destroys fear. (11)
There is no disease equal to desire, no enemy equal to delusion, no fire equal to anger, and there is no happiness higher than knowledge. 12.
For one alone undergoes birth and death; one alone experiences the auspicious and the inauspicious;
one alone falls into the hells, and one alone attains the supreme goal. (13)
To the knower of Brahman, heaven is as a blade of grass; to the hero, life is as a blade of grass;
to the one who has conquered his senses, a woman is as a blade of grass; and to the one free from desire, the entire world is as a blade of grass. (14)
Knowledge is a friend during travels, and a wife is a friend in the home;
medicine is a friend to the sick, and dharma is a friend to the deceased. (15)
Rain upon the oceans is in vain; food for those who are already satiated is in vain;
a gift to the wealthy is in vain; and a lamp where there is no darkness is also in vain. (16)
There is no water equal to the clouds; there is no strength equal to one's own self; there is no brilliance equal to the eyes; there is no object as dear as grain. 17.
The destitute desire wealth; four-footed creatures desire speech;
human beings desire heaven; and the gods desire liberation. (18)
By truth the earth is supported; by truth the sun gives heat;
by truth the wind blows; everything is established in truth. 19.
Fortune is fickle, the vital breaths are fickle, and life in this body is fickle;
in this world where everything is unstable, Dharma alone is indeed immovable. (20)
Among men, the barber is the rogue; among birds, the crow;
among quadrupeds, the jackal; and among women, Mālinī is the rogue.
The progenitor, the one who performs the initiation ceremony, the one who imparts knowledge, the giver of food, and the protector from fear—these five are remembered as fathers. ||22||
The wife of a king, the wife of a teacher, the wife of a friend, as well as the wife of one’s own brother, and one’s mother—these five are remembered as mothers. (23)
The Sixth Chapter:
By hearing, one understands the Dharma; by hearing, one abandons evil-mindedness;
by hearing, one attains knowledge; by hearing, one may attain liberation. ||1||
Among birds, the crow is the outcaste; among animals, the dog;
and among sages, the sinful man who reviles all outcastes is the outcaste. (2)
Bell-metal is purified by ash; copper is purified by acid;
a woman is purified by her menses; and a river is purified by its current. (3)
A king is honored when he wanders; a twice-born man is honored when he wanders;
a yogi is honored when he wanders; but a woman perishes when she wanders. ||4||
He who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen.
He who has wealth is a man in this world, and he who has wealth is a wise man.
The intellect arises as such, the resolve is likewise such, and the companions are exactly such as the destiny that is to be. (6)
Time ripens all beings; Time destroys all creatures.
Time remains awake while others sleep; indeed, Time is difficult to overcome. (7)
One blinded by desire does not see their own downfall;
those intoxicated by pride do not see; and one who is greedy for wealth does not see his own faults. (8)
The self performs the action itself; the self experiences its fruit itself;
the self wanders in saṃsāra itself; and the self is liberated from it itself. (9)
The king [incurs] the sin committed by the kingdom; the domestic priest, the sin of the king;
the husband, the sin committed by his wife; and likewise the teacher, the sin of the disciple. (10)
A father who incurs debt is an enemy; a mother who is unfaithful is an enemy;
a beautiful wife is an enemy; and an unlearned son is an enemy. (11)
One should win over the greedy with wealth, the stubborn with a gesture of salutation (joined palms),
the fool by following his whims, and the wise man by speaking the truth.

Better than sovereignty is not to have a kingdom, better than a kingdom is not to have the kingdom of a bad king; better than a friend is not to have a friend, better than a friend is not to have the friendship of a bad friend; better than a disciple is not to have a disciple, better than a disciple is not to have the discipleship of a bad disciple.
Better is no wife at all than a bad wife. ||13||
How can there be happiness for the subjects under a wicked king’s rule?
How can there be fulfillment with a bad friend as a friend? And how can there be delight in the home with a bad wife as a wife?
For one who teaches an unworthy disciple, whence can there be fame? ||14||
One should learn one thing from the lion, one from the crane, four from the cock, five from the crow, six from the dog, and three from the donkey. (15)
Even if a man desires to accomplish a task that is vast, he accomplishes that task with total exertion; this alone is said to be the quality of a lion. (16)
And having restrained his senses like a crane, a wise man, knowing the proper place, time, and strength, should accomplish all his tasks. (17)
One should learn four things from a cock: rising up [to greet], fighting, sharing with kinsmen, and eating only after having attacked [the food] oneself. //18//
One should learn five things from the crow: secrecy in sexual conduct, gathering at the proper times, vigilance, and mistrust. (19)
Eating much, being easily satisfied, sleeping soundly, having light-mindedness, devotion to the master, and being brave—these six are the qualities of a dog. (20)
Though exhausted, it carries its burden and perceives neither cold nor heat;
being ever contented, one should learn these three things from the donkey.
The man who practices these twenty qualities will be invincible in all circumstances of action.
Chapter Seven: A wise person should not disclose the loss of wealth, mental anguish, the conduct of one's wife, the speech of the base, or insults. (1)
In the employment of wealth and grain, in the acquisition of knowledge, in eating, and in worldly dealings, one who has cast aside shame shall be happy. (2)
The happiness and peace that belong to those satisfied by the nectar of contentment do not belong to those greedy for wealth, who run hither and thither.
Contentment should be practiced in three matters: regarding one's own wife, food, and wealth;
but it should not be practiced in these three: study, recitation, and giving.
One should not pass between two Brahmins, nor between a husband and wife, nor between a master and a servant, nor between a plow and its oxen.
One should not touch with one's feet fire, a teacher, or a Brahmin;
nor indeed a cow, a young girl, an elder, or likewise a child.
An elephant [is driven away] by a thousand cubits, a horse by a hundred cubits, a horned beast by ten cubits, and a wicked person by the abandonment of the country. (7)
An elephant is controlled by a mere goad, and a horse is struck with a hand;
a horned beast is subdued with a staff in hand, but a wicked person is not tamed by a sword in hand.
Brahmins find satisfaction in food, peacocks in the thundering of clouds; the virtuous rejoice in the prosperity of others, while the wicked rejoice in the misfortunes of others.
An enemy who is stronger [should be approached] in a conciliatory manner, one of inferior birth in a hostile manner, and an enemy of equal strength through discipline or force. (10)
The strength of a king is the power of his arm; the strength of one who knows Brahman is wisdom; and for women, beauty, youth, and sweetness are the unsurpassed strength. 11.
One should not remain excessively upright; go and look at the forest land!
There the straight trees are cut down, while the crooked trees remain standing. 12.
Where there is water, there the swans dwell; likewise, they avoid that which is dry. A man should not be like a swan, repeatedly abandoning and repeatedly resorting [to others]. (13)
Indeed, the relinquishing of accumulated wealth is its true preservation, just as the overflow of waters contained within the belly of a reservoir is its protection. 14.
He who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen. He who has wealth is a man in this world; he who has wealth truly lives. (15)
For those residing in heaven, four signs remain in their bodies within the world of the living:
a devotion to giving and sweet speech.
Worship of the gods and the gratification of Brahmins. ||16||
Excessive anger, harsh speech,
poverty, enmity toward one's own kin, association with the base, and service to those of low birth.
These are the marks on the bodies of those residing in hell. ||17||
If one goes to the palace of the lord of beasts (the lion),
one obtains the pearls from the temples of elephants; yet,
when one has gone to the abode of jackals, what is obtained?
The tearing of the hide of a donkey used as a seat-cover. ||18||
Life without knowledge is as useless as a dog's tail;
it is neither capable of guarding secrets nor of warding off bites. (19)
Purity of speech, purity of mind, restraint of the senses, and compassion toward all beings—this is purity; this is the purity of those who seek the highest goal. (20)
As fragrance is in a flower, oil in sesame seeds, fire in wood, milk in [the udder], and ghee in [milk];
as sugar is in sugarcane—so behold the Self within the body through discernment. 21.
The Eighth Chapter:
Inferior people desire wealth; middling people desire both wealth and honor;
superior people desire honor alone, for honor is indeed the wealth of the great. (1)
Even after consuming sugarcane, water, milk, roots, betel leaf, fruit, or medicine,
the rites of bathing, giving gifts, and so forth must still be performed.
A lamp consumes darkness and produces soot;
whatever food is constantly eaten, such offspring is born. (3)
O wise one, bestow wealth upon those endowed with virtue; do not give it elsewhere.
Just as the water of the ocean, when released by the clouds, is always imbued with sweetness, so too do all living beings, both mobile and immobile, sustain the entire circle of the earth.
Behold once more that very ocean, multiplied ten million times; go there yourself.
Even by thousands of Cāṇḍālas and by wise seers who perceive the truth, a single Yavana is indeed declared to be low; there is no one more base than a Yavana. (5)
After anointing with oil, exposure to the smoke of a funeral pyre, sexual intercourse, or the act of shaving,
one remains an outcaste (cāṇḍāla) until one performs a ritual bath.
Water is medicine when food is undigested; water bestows strength when digestion is complete.
Water is nectar during a meal, but at the end of a meal, it is poison. (7)
Knowledge devoid of action is lost, and a man is ruined by ignorance;
an army without a leader is destroyed, for women are indeed lost when they have no husband. (8)
A wife who dies in old age, wealth that has fallen into the hands of kinsmen, and a vessel dependent on others—these are the mockeries of men. 9.
Without the Agnihotra sacrifice, the Vedas are of no avail; without charity, there are no rites; without devotion, there is no success; therefore, devotion is indeed the cause.
The deity is not found in wood, nor in stone, nor in clay;
for the deity is found in devotion (bhāva), therefore devotion is indeed the cause.
By performing service with devotion using materials such as wood, stone, or clay, and through that very faith, one attains success by the grace of Viṣṇu. (12)
There is no austerity equal to tranquility; there is no happiness greater than contentment; there is no disease worse than craving; and there is no dharma higher than compassion. 13.
Anger is Yama, the son of Vivasvat; craving is the river Vaitaraṇī;
knowledge is the wish-fulfilling cow; and contentment is the Nandana grove. (14)
Virtue adorns physical beauty; character adorns one's lineage; success adorns learning; and the enjoyer adorns wealth. (15)
The form of one devoid of virtue is ruined; the family of one of ill-conduct is ruined; the learning of one who does not practice it is ruined; and wealth through lack of enjoyment is ruined. (16)
Water on the ground is pure; a woman devoted to her husband is pure;
a king who ensures security is pure; and a contented Brāhmaṇa is pure. (17)

The twice-born have perished through lack of contentment, and kings through excessive contentment; the courtesan has perished through modesty, and the woman of noble family through shamelessness. (18)
Of what use is a vast lineage for embodied beings if it is devoid of learning? Even one from a low family who is wise is indeed honored by the gods. (19)
The learned man is praised in the world; the learned man receives respect everywhere. Through knowledge one obtains everything; knowledge is honored everywhere. (20)
Those endowed with beauty and youth, born of a noble lineage, do not shine if devoid of learning, like *kiṃśuka* flowers without fragrance. (21)
The earth is oppressed by the weight of those who eat meat, those who drink liquor, fools devoid of learning, and beasts in human form. (22)
A sacrifice lacking food burns the kingdom; one lacking mantras ruins the ṛṣis and the officiating priests;
and one lacking gifts ruins the patron. There is no enemy equal to a sacrifice [performed thus]. 23.
The Ninth Chapter:
O dear one! If you desire liberation, abandon sense-objects like poison;
drink in forgiveness, straightforwardness, compassion, purity, and truth as if they were nectar. (1)
Those lowest of men who speak of each other's vital secrets meet their own destruction, like snakes within the belly of an anthill.
Fragrance was produced for gold by the stalks of fruit-bearing sugarcane, and indeed, flowers were made from sandalwood.
A learned man, a wealthy man, a king, and one who lives long—none of these elements existed in the past as bestowers of wisdom. (3)
Among all medicinal herbs, nectar is preeminent; among all pleasures, food is preeminent;
among all the sense faculties, the eye is preeminent.
Among all the limbs, the head is the most important.
A messenger does not travel through the sky, nor can news move without him.
This was not spoken before, nor has there been a meeting.
How can that best of the twice-born not be considered wise, who knows the auspicious occurrence of the eclipses of the sun and moon situated in the sky? ||5||
A student, a servant, a traveler, one afflicted by hunger, one terrified by fear, a treasurer, and a doorkeeper—these seven should be awakened from sleep. (6)
One should not awaken these seven who are sleeping: a snake, a king, a tiger, a child, a bride, a dog, and a fool.
Those twice-born ones by whom the Vedas have been studied for their material gain, and who eat the food of Śūdras—what will they accomplish? They are like venomless serpents. (8)
When he is angry there is no fear, and when he is pleased there is no acquisition of wealth; since he possesses neither the power to punish nor to favor, what will he do when he is enraged? (9)
Even a snake devoid of venom must display a great hood;
whether it possesses poison or not, its swelling hood is terrifying.
Through the pursuit of learning, through engagement with women at midday, and through the pursuit of thieves at night, time passes for the wise. (11)
A garland strung by one's own hand, sandalwood paste ground by one's own hand, and a painting drawn by one's own hand—these would take away the splendor even of Śakra himself. (12)
Sugarcane stalks, sesame seeds, Śūdras, a beloved wife, gold that brings joy, sandalwood, curd, betel leaf, and massage increase one's virtues.
Poverty shines through fortitude;
the wearing of poor clothing shines through purity.
Bad food shines because of its warmth; ugliness shines because of one's virtuous conduct. ||14||
The Tenth Chapter: Now begins the latter half of the *Vṛddha-Cāṇakya*.
One who is destitute of wealth is not truly lowly; he who possesses wealth is certainly high-born.
He who is devoid of the jewel of knowledge is destitute of all things. ||1||
One should place one's foot down purified by sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by scripture; and one should act with a mind that is purified. ||2||
One who seeks pleasure should abandon knowledge; one who seeks knowledge should abandon pleasure.
For one who seeks pleasure, whence can there be knowledge? And for one who seeks knowledge, whence can there be pleasure? (3)
What do poets not see? What do women not do?
What do drunkards not prattle? And what do crows not eat? (4)
Fate makes a king a pauper and a pauper a king; likewise, it makes the wealthy poor and the poor wealthy. (5)
To the greedy, a beggar is an enemy; to fools, one who imparts knowledge is an enemy;
to unfaithful wives, a husband is an enemy; and to thieves, the moon is an enemy.
Those who possess neither knowledge nor austerity, neither generosity nor ethical conduct, neither virtue nor righteousness,
are a burden upon this earth in the world of mortals.
Deer roam about in human form. ||7||
Instruction does not take root in those who lack inner substance;
through contact with the Malaya mountain, a bamboo stalk does not become sandalwood.
What can a treatise do for one who lacks wisdom within themselves?
What will a mirror avail one who is deprived of eyes? (9)
There is indeed no means on this earth to turn a wicked person into a virtuous one;
even if the anus were washed a hundred times, it would not become a superior organ. (10)
From hatred toward one's preceptor comes death; from hatred toward others, the loss of wealth;
from hatred toward the king, ruin; and from hatred toward a Brahmin, the destruction of the lineage. (11)
Better is the forest inhabited by tigers and lordly elephants, with dwellings among the trees, where one subsists on ripe fruit and water,
sleeps upon the grass, and wears a hundred-worn garment of bark.
One does not lead a life destitute of wealth in the midst of kinsmen. ||12||
The Brahmin is a tree; its root is the twilight prayers (sandhyā), its branches are the Vedas, and its leaves are the acts of dharma.
Therefore, one must strive to protect the root.
When the root is severed, there are neither branches nor leaves. ||13||
Mother is the goddess Kamalā, father is Lord Janārdana, and kinsmen are the devotees of Viṣṇu; one's own country is the three worlds. (14)
When birds of various colors have perched upon a single tree at dawn, what cause for lamentation is there in the ten directions? ||15||
He whose intellect is his strength—how can there be strength for those devoid of intellect? An elephant in rut was brought down in the forest by a hare. (16)
He whose intellect is his strength—how can there be strength for those devoid of intellect?
In the forest, an elephant intoxicated with rut was brought down by a hare. (16)
What concern is mine for my own life, if Hari is sung of as the sustainer of the universe?
Otherwise, how could the mother’s milk flow forth for the life of her infant?
Having reflected thus again and again, O Lord of the Yadus, O Lord of Lakṣmī, I shall spend my time forever solely in the service of Your lotus feet. (17)
Although my intellect is distinguished regarding the speech of the gods (Sanskrit), I am nevertheless eager for other languages;
just as there is a longing for the nectar of the lips of celestial nymphs even when the nectar of immortality exists among the gods. 18.
Flour is ten times more [efficacious] than rice; milk is ten times more than flour;
meat is eight times more than milk; and ghee is ten times more than meat. (19)
Diseases increase through leafy vegetables; the body increases through milk;
virility increases through ghee; and flesh increases through meat. (20)
Chapter Eleven:
Generosity, pleasant speech, fortitude, and discernment of what is appropriate—these four innate qualities are not acquired through practice. (1)
Having abandoned one's own party, if one should take refuge in another's party, one perishes by one's own hand, just as a kingdom does through unrighteousness. ||2||
An elephant has a massive body, yet it is subject to the control of a mere goad;
when a lamp is lit, darkness perishes, yet is darkness merely the lamp?
Even mountains struck by the thunderbolt fall; are mountains merely [made of] thunderbolts?
He whose splendor shines forth is the one truly powerful; the one who shoots a thick arrow is merely a source of confidence.
Hari abandons the earth for ten thousand kalpas;
half of that time is spent in the waters of the Gaṅgā, and half of that is spent as a village deity. (4)
For one attached to home there is no knowledge; for a consumer of meat there is no compassion;
for one greedy for wealth there is no truth; and for one devoted to women there is no purity. (5)
A wicked person does not attain the state of a virtuous one, even when being instructed in many ways;
a neem tree, though watered at its roots with milk and ghee, does not attain sweetness.
A wicked person with impurity within is not purified even by hundreds of ritual baths at sacred fords,
just as a vessel that has been smeared with wine is not cleansed even when burnt.

He who does not know the excellence of another's qualities always censures him; there is nothing surprising in this, just as a crow, having obtained [a morsel] from the temple-frontal globes of an elephant, [caws at it].
Having abandoned the pearl, he wears the guñjā berry.
But those who always eat in silence for a full year are honored in the heavenly world for thousands of crores of yugas. ||9||
One who seeks knowledge should indeed avoid these eight: lust, anger, greed, attachment to delicious tastes, vanity, curiosity, excessive sleep, and over-indulgence in worldly pleasures. (10)
One who daily performs the ancestral rites with roots and fruits grown without cultivation from forest streams is called a brahmin sage (ṛṣi). ||11||
Content with eating but one meal a day, always devoted to the six duties, and approaching his wife only during her season—that Brāhmaṇa is called a twice-born. 12.
He who is devoted to worldly occupations, who protects cattle, and who engages in trade and agriculture—that Brahmin is indeed called a Vaiśya. (13)
A Brahmin who sells lac and other such substances, oils, indigo, saffron, honey, clarified butter, liquor, or meat is called a Śūdra.
A Brahmin who thwarts the affairs of others, who is hypocritical, who achieves his own ends, who is deceitful, hateful, and both mild and cruel, is called a cat. (15)
That Brahmin who destroys ponds, wells, tanks, groves, and temples without any hesitation is called a Mleccha. (16)

One who misappropriates the property of the gods or the property of the guru, who violates the wife of another, and who fails to provide sustenance for all living beings—a Brahmin such as this is called a Caṇḍāla. (17)
The wealth of food should be given away by those of virtuous deeds; its accumulation brings no glory.
Even today, the fame of Śrīkarṇa and Vikramāditya, the lord of power, endures;
whereas our long-accumulated store, devoid of the enjoyment of giving honey, has perished.
"Alas! These flies are rubbing their pair of lost legs against [the ground] as if it were Nirvana! ||18||
The twelfth chapter:
A joyful home, sons endowed with wisdom, a beloved wife who speaks sweetly,
wealth that fulfills all desires, delight in one's own wife, and servants devoted to one’s commands.
Hospitality, the daily worship of Śiva, sweet food and drink in the home, and the constant service of virtuous guests—blessed indeed is the householder's stage of life! ||1||
If one endowed with compassion gives even a small amount of a gift with faith to distressed brahmins,
that gift attains infinite and boundless merit;
what is given to them cannot be recovered from the twice-born.
Courtesy toward one's own kin, compassion for strangers, constant guile toward the wicked, affection for the virtuous, pride before the base, and straightforwardness toward the learned;
valor toward enemies, forbearance toward elders, and craftiness toward women.
Thus, the stability of the world rests upon those men who are skilled in the arts. ||3||
My two hands are devoid of giving; my ears are enemies of sacred learning; my eyes are bereft of beholding the virtuous; and my feet have never traveled to a holy place.
O jackal, quickly release, release this vile and utterly contemptible body—its belly filled with wealth acquired through injustice and its head held high with pride! (4)
Those men who possess no devotion for the lotus feet of the illustrious son of Yaśodā; whose palates are not enamored with the narration of the virtues of the beloved of the cowherd girls;
and whose ears do not respectfully listen to the charmingly sweet stories of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s divine play—[for them, this world is a waste].
Fie on that drum! Fie on it, fie! Fie on this drum that constantly proclaims [the name] through its chanting and hymns! ||5||
When there is no leaf at all on the *karīra* tree, is that the fault of spring?
If the owl does not see even by day, is that a defect of the sun? When rain does not fall into the mouth of the *cātaka* bird, is that the fault of the cloud?
Who is capable of erasing that which was previously inscribed on the forehead by destiny? ||6||
Indeed, goodness arises in the wicked through association with the virtuous; but goodness does not become wickedness in the virtuous through association with the wicked.
Only the earth possesses the fragrance born of flowers;
the flowers themselves do not retain the scent of the earth. ||7||
Beholding the virtuous is meritorious, for the virtuous are themselves sacred pilgrimage sites;
a pilgrimage site bears fruit in time, but the company of the virtuous yields fruit immediately. (8)
O Brahmin, in this city there is a great multitude of palm trees that tell stories;
who is a donor? The washerman, who gives back the garment after having taken it at night; who is skillful? Every person is skillful at seizing the wealth and wives of others.
"Why do you live, O friend? "I live by the logic of the worm in poison. (9)
There were no lotuses for washing the feet of Brahmins, nor the thundering resonance of the Vedas and Shastras,
and they were entirely devoid of the utterances of "Svaha" and "Svadha."
Those houses are equal to cremation grounds. ||10||
Truth is my mother, knowledge my father, righteousness my brother, compassion my friend, peace my wife, and forgiveness my son; these six are my kinsmen. 11.
Bodies are impermanent and worldly prosperity is never eternal;
death is ever-present, so one must practice the accumulation of Dharma. (12)
Brahmins rejoice in invitations, cows rejoice in fresh grass, and a wife rejoices in her husband’s enthusiasm; O Kṛṣṇa! I rejoice in battle.
He who looks upon the wives of others as his own mother, the property of others as a clod of earth, and all living beings as himself—he is a wise man. 14.
Devotion to the Dharma, sweetness of speech, enthusiasm for giving, sincerity toward friends, humility toward the guru, profound depth of mind,
purity in conduct, appreciation of virtue, and mastery of the scriptures.
Beauty resides in form, devotion in Śiva, and yet Rāghava exists within you. ||15||
The wish-fulfilling tree is but wood; Mount Sumeru is a mere mountain; the wish-granting gem is a stone;
the sun has scorching rays; the moon causes its own waning; the ocean is but salt water;
Kāma is bodiless; Bali, the son of Diti, is eternally a beast; and those who move at will are but slaves to their desires.
O Lord of the Raghus, I do not compare you to those; to whom could you possibly be likened?
Knowledge is a friend during travel, and a wife is a friend in the home;
medicine is a friend to one who is ill, and dharma is a friend to the deceased. (17)
One should learn discipline from princes, eloquent speech from the wise, falsehood from gamblers, and guile from women. (18)
A man who spends without regard for his income, who is without a protector, who is fond of quarreling, and who is distressed in all matters concerning women and his fields, perishes quickly. (19)
A wise person should not think of food; rather, he should think only of dharma.
For food is born together with the birth of human beings.
In the investment of wealth and grain, in the acquisition of knowledge, as well as in eating and worldly dealings, one who has cast aside shame shall find happiness. (21)
A jar is filled gradually by the falling of drops of water;
that is the cause of all branches of knowledge, as well as of righteousness and wealth. (22)
Even in the decline of age, he who is wicked remains indeed wicked; even when fully ripened, the *indravāruṇa* gourd does not lose its bitterness.
Chapter Thirteen:
A man should live for even a single moment by means of pure action;
he should not live for an entire kalpa through painful toil that opposes the interests of both worlds.
One should not grieve for what has passed, nor should one worry about the future;
the wise conduct themselves according to the present time. (2)
For gods, virtuous men, and fathers are satisfied by one's inherent nature;
kinsmen by bathing and drinking; and the wise by the gift of speech. (3)
Lifespan, karma, wealth, knowledge, and even death—these five are created for the embodied being while still dwelling in the womb. (4)
Oh, how wondrous indeed are the deeds of the great-souled!
They regard fortune as a mere blade of grass, yet they bow under its weight. (5)
For whom there is affection, for him there is fear; affection is a vessel of suffering.
Sufferings have their root in affection; having abandoned them, one may dwell in happiness. (6)
The one who provides for the future and the one with presence of mind—these two prosper in happiness, while the fatalist perishes. (7)
When the king is righteous, the subjects are righteous; when he is sinful, they are sinful; when he is neutral, they are neutral.
The subjects follow the king; as is the king, so are the subjects. (8)
I consider an embodied being devoid of dharma to be dead even while living;
one who has died endowed with dharma is a long-lived person, there is no doubt.
He for whom even one among dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa does not exist has a birth as useless as the fleshy nipple on the neck of a goat. (10)
Being scorched by the exceedingly intense fire of another's fame, the base, being unable to reach that same state, engage in slander. (11)
Attachment to sense objects leads to bondage; the mind free from sense objects leads to liberation.
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings. 12.
When the identification with the body has dissolved through knowledge of the Supreme Self, wherever the mind goes, there are states of meditative absorption. //13//
For whom does every desired happiness of the mind come to pass? Since everything depends upon destiny, one should therefore take refuge in contentment. 14.
Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows, so too does whatever action has been performed follow after the doer. (15)
For one whose mind is unsettled, there is no happiness either among people or in the forest;
people burn through association, while the forest [burns] through the abandonment of attachment. 16.
Just as one who digs into the earth with a spade finds water, so too does the diligent student acquire the knowledge residing in the teacher. 17.
The fruit of human beings depends upon their karma, and the intellect follows that karma;
nevertheless, the wise and noble act only after having reflected well. (18)
He who does not pay homage to the guru who has bestowed even a single syllable upon him, after passing through a hundred births as a dog, is born among the Cāṇḍālas. (19)
At the end of a yuga, Mount Meru may shake; at the end of a kalpa, the seven oceans may overflow;
but the virtuous never waver from the goal they have undertaken.
On this earth there are three jewels: food, water, and well-spoken words;
yet by fools, the designation of "jewel" is applied to mere fragments of stone. (21)
The Fourteenth Chapter:
These are the fruits for embodied beings of the tree of one's own transgressions:
poverty, disease, suffering, imprisonment, and calamities. (1)
Wealth can be regained, friends can be regained, a wife can be regained, and the earth can be regained; all these may be obtained again, but the body cannot be regained again and again. (2)
Even a multitude of beings, when united, can conquer their enemies;
yet a cloud raining down torrents is warded off even by blades of grass. (3)

Oil spreads upon water; a secret reaches even a wicked person; a gift, however small, reaches a worthy recipient; and a scripture reaches a wise man—by the very nature of things, each expands of its own accord. ||4||
If the state of mind that arises in a discourse on the Dharma, in a cremation ground, or among the sick were to persist at all times, who would not be liberated from bondage? (5)
If one possessed such an understanding beforehand as the understanding that arises in one who has already developed remorse, who would not attain great success? (6)
One should not feel astonishment at generosity, austerity, heroism, specialized knowledge, discipline, or statesmanship; for the earth abounds in many jewels.
Even one who stands nearby is far away if he does not dwell in another's mind;
but he who is in another's heart is close, even if standing at a distance.
And because one who desires what is dear should always speak what is dear to that person, the hunter sings a sweet-sounding song in order to go after the killing of deer. (9)
Those who are too close lead to destruction, while those who remain at a distance yield no fruit;
therefore, one should attend upon kings, sacred fires, teachers, and women by maintaining a middle course. (10)
Fire, water, women, fools, serpents, and royal courts—these six must always be approached with great caution, for they can take one's life instantly. (11)
He lives who possesses virtues; he lives who possesses righteousness.
For one devoid of virtue and righteousness, life is purposeless.
If you wish to bring the world under your control by a single deed, then restrain the cow from grazing before these fifteen-faced ones. (13)
He who knows how to speak words appropriate to the occasion, to give what is pleasing in accordance with his power, and to exercise anger in proportion to his own strength, is a wise man. (14)
A single object indeed is perceived in three ways: as a corpse by yogis, as a woman of desire by lovers, and as meat by dogs. (15)
A wise person should not disclose a well-prepared medicine, a religious practice, a domestic secret, sexual intercourse, bad eating, or improper learning. (16)
The days are spent in silence by the cuckoos until their voice, which bestows joy upon all people, begins to flow. (17)
Dharma, wealth, grain, the word of the guru, and medicine must be properly grasped; otherwise, one does not survive. (18)
Abandon association with the wicked; cultivate the company of the virtuous.
Perform meritorious deeds day and night, and constantly remember the impermanence of all things. 19.
Fifteenth Chapter:
For one whose heart has melted with compassion toward all living beings, what need is there for knowledge or liberation through matted hair and the smearing of ashes? (1)
If a teacher awakens a disciple to even a single syllable, there is no object on earth that, by giving it, one could become free from debt. ||2||
There are only two ways to deal with the wicked and thorns:
wearing shoes, cutting off their tips, or simply keeping them at a distance. (3)
One who wears tattered rags, who bears the grime of teeth, who eats excessively, who speaks harshly,
and who sleeps at sunrise or sunset— [these are not to be honored].
If Śrī, the wielder of the discus, were to abandon him. ||4||
Friends, wives, servants, and well-wishers abandon one who is destitute of wealth;
yet they resort once again to that same person when he possesses riches.
For in this world, wealth is indeed the kinsman of a man. ||5||
Wealth acquired by unjust means remains for ten years;
when the eleventh year arrives, it perishes along with its very roots.
What is improper for a master is proper for a servant; what is proper for a base person is a reproach.
Nectar was death to Rāhu, while poison became the ornament of Śaṅkara. (7)
That is true food which is the remnant of what has been eaten by the twice-born;
that is true friendship which is extended toward another;
that is true wisdom which commits no evil.
That which is performed without hypocrisy is sin; that which is performed without hypocrisy is dharma. ||8||
The jewel rolls at the feet while the glass is worn upon the head;
yet at the time of purchase and sale, the glass is glass and the jewel is a jewel.
The scriptures are infinite and the branches of knowledge are many;
time is short and obstacles are numerous.
Therefore, that which constitutes the essence should be cultivated.
Just as a swan [extracts] milk from the midst of water. ||10||
He who eats without honoring a guest who has come from afar, who is weary from the road, and who has come to his house in vain, is indeed called a Cāṇḍāla. 11.
They recite the four Vedas and the treatises on Dharma many times over,
yet they do not know the Self at all, just as one who has cooked a dish does not perceive its own flavor.
Blessed is the boat consisting of the twice-born, which is turned upside down in the ocean of worldly existence;
all those situated below cross over, while those standing above fall down. 13.
This leader is a treasury of nectar and even among medicinal herbs;
he is the moon, possessing a body composed of nectar and endowed with splendor.
The orb of the sun becomes devoid of its rays upon reaching the sun itself;
who does not fall into insignificance when entering another's house? (14)
This bee, dwelling amidst the petals of a lotus and languid with intoxication from the nectar of the water-lily,
has by the power of fate arrived in a foreign land.
He highly values the juice of the *kuṭaja* flower. ||15||

O Lord, my father was turned yellow by his anger when struck by the sole of your foot; my beloved husband, out of wrath, has held my enemy within the cavity of his mouth since childhood along with the best of Brahmins;
and they destroy my home every day for the sake of worshipping Umā’s consort. Therefore, O Protector, I am constantly distressed and it is right that I abandon this abode of the twice-born. 16.
Indeed, there are many kinds of bonds; the bond formed by the cord of affection is of another sort.
Even an axe, though skilled at splitting wood, becomes motionless when it encounters the sheath of a lotus. (17)
Even when cut down, the sandalwood tree does not abandon its fragrance; even when grown large, the lordly elephant does not abandon his grace;
and even when placed upon a machine, the sugarcane does not abandon its sweetness.
Even when impoverished, a person of noble birth does not abandon the virtues of moral conduct. ||18||
On this earth, some great mountain was held effortlessly with two hands;
for that reason, you are celebrated as Govardhana throughout heaven and on the ground.
That I carry you, the upholder of the three worlds, upon the tips of my breasts is counted as nothing.
Or what is the use of much speaking, O Keśava? Fame is obtained through meritorious deeds. ||19||
